prompt.context: Your client is PrimeCo, a major producer and distributor of advanced industrial products. Advanced industrials refers to products with technically complex design and manufacturing processes, including industries like advanced electronics, aerospace and defense, and automotive assembly. PrimeCo is one of the largest aerospace and defense prime contractors — a prime contractor is the firm hired to complete the final product and fulfill the order contract. PrimeCo sells finished products to both the U.S. government and private sector clients, and has both its headquarters and all manufacturing operations in the U.S.
prompt.question: The CEO of PrimeCo has hired your firm to investigate why PrimeCo's profits have been declining, and to recommend solutions to improve their situation.

clarifying_info.a: A prime contractor is the firm hired to complete the final product and fulfill the order contract.

A sub-component is an item assembled by a subcontractor (supplier) and sold to PrimeCo, who then uses it as one part of the final product. For example, GM may purchase already assembled brake pads from Callahan Automotive.
PrimeCo has both its headquarters and all manufacturing operations in the U.S.
PrimeCo sells finished products to both the U.S. government and private sector clients.

exhibits.title: PrimeCo Historical Financials
exhibits.shows: A bar chart comparing PrimeCo's annual revenue and profit (in $M) from 2008 to 2015

exhibits.title: PrimeCo Cost Structure
exhibits.shows: Two pie charts showing PrimeCo's cost breakdown by category in 2012 and 2015

exhibits.title: SubPrime Co Product Breakdown and Market Analysis
exhibits.shows: Three panels: (1) a cost teardown of Sub-component #3 priced at $10.00/unit showing percentage breakdown by part, labor, overhead, and profit; (2) worldwide market prices for Part A, Part B, and Part C; (3) profit margin and overhead rate benchmarks for three competitors

framework: Understand the profitability issue: revenue trend vs. profit trend over time
Decompose costs: identify which cost categories have grown disproportionately
Drill into Sub-component #3: analyze the supplier (SubPrime Co) cost structure
Benchmark SubPrime Co against market prices and competitor overhead/margins
Quantify the impact of renegotiating the sub-component price on PrimeCo profits
Assess strategic and financial implications of helping SubPrime Co improve operations

questions.prompt: Look at Exhibit 1. What do you observe about PrimeCo's financial performance, and what would you like to investigate next?
questions.guidance: Strong answer: Revenue has grown steadily from $327M (2008) to $700M (2015). Profit also grew from 2008 to 2012 but has been declining for the past three years despite continued revenue growth. Profit margin has dropped significantly — from roughly 90% in 2008 to ~57% in 2015 (400/700). This signals a cost problem, not a revenue problem. Candidate should want to dig into the cost structure.

math.setup: Profit margin 2008 = 293/327 ≈ 90%; Profit margin 2015 = 400/700 ≈ 57%. Total costs 2012 = 545 - 488 = $57M. Total costs 2015 = 700 - 400 = $300M.
math.answer: Profit margin has compressed from ~90% to ~57%; total costs grew from $57M to $300M while revenue grew from $545M to $700M.

questions.prompt: Look at Exhibit 2. What stands out about PrimeCo's cost structure between 2012 and 2015?
questions.guidance: Strong answer: Sub-component #3 has increased dramatically as a proportion of total costs, from 25% in 2012 to 39% in 2015. Manufacturing labor dropped from 22% to 14% and distribution from 14% to 11%, possibly due to automation or efficiency gains. The spike in Sub-component #3 is the primary driver of rising costs and declining profit. Candidate should want to investigate the Sub-component #3 supplier.

math.setup: Sub-component #3 in dollar terms: 2012 = 25% x $57M; 2015 = 39% x $300M
math.answer: Sub-component #3 spend grew from $14.25M to $117M — an increase of $102.75M.

questions.prompt: Look at Exhibit 3. What can you determine about SubPrime Co's pricing of Sub-component #3? (Unit price is $10.00)
questions.guidance: Strong answer: Calculate the dollar amount of each line item. Compare Part A and Part C actual prices to worldwide market prices. Note SubPrime Co's overhead rate vs. competitors. Sub-component #3 at $10/unit breaks down as: Part A = $1.00 (market $0.83 — marked up); Part B = $0.80 (market $0.85 — PrimeCo getting a deal); Part C = $3.33 (market $3.12 — marked up); Labor = $2.68; Overhead = $0.99; Profit = $1.20. SubPrime Co's overhead rate is 9.9% vs. competitor average ~3.0% — significantly above industry. Profit margin at 12% is below competitors' ~15%. Candidate should note SubPrime Co is overcharging on Parts A and C, and has bloated overhead.

math.setup: Multiply each % by $10.00 unit price to get dollar amounts; compare parts to market prices
steps: Part A: 10% x $10 = $1.00 vs. market $0.83 (markup of $0.17)
Part B: 8% x $10 = $0.80 vs. market $0.85 (discount of $0.05)
Part C: 33.3% x $10 = $3.33 vs. market $3.12 (markup of $0.21)
Overhead: 9.9% x $10 = $0.99 (competitors average ~3.0% = ~$0.27 at same base)
math.answer: SubPrime Co charges $1.00 for Part A (market $0.83) and $3.33 for Part C (market $3.12). Overhead at 9.9% is 3x competitor average. Profit margin at 12% is below industry.

questions.prompt: Question 1 (Prompt 2): PrimeCo proposes a deal — if SubPrime Co lowers unit price to $9.00, PrimeCo will help them source Parts A, B, C at worldwide market prices and share manufacturing best practices. The new $9.00 price will include parts at market prices, overhead at industry average (3.0%), and profit margin at industry average (15.0%). By how much (in dollars) will SubPrime Co have to reduce labor costs per unit to achieve this $9.00/unit price?
questions.guidance: Candidate must build a new cost structure at $9.00/unit using the given constraints, then solve for the required labor cost. Parts are sourced at market prices; overhead drops to 3.0% of $9.00 = $0.27; profit rises to 15% of $9.00 = $1.35. Sum up known items and subtract from $9.00 to find new labor. Then compare to old labor ($2.68) to find the reduction required.

math.setup: New unit price = $9.00. Parts at market: A=$0.83, B=$0.85, C=$3.12. Overhead = 3.0% x $9.00 = $0.27. Profit = 15.0% x $9.00 = $1.35. Solve for Labor.
math.answer: SubPrime Co must reduce labor costs by $0.10 per unit (from $2.68 to $2.58).

questions.prompt: Question 2 (Prompt 2): If this price decrease returned PrimeCo's spend on Sub-component #3 to 2012 levels ($14.25M), how would this impact PrimeCo's 2015 profits? Assume no changes to revenue or other costs.
questions.guidance: Candidate should use previously derived figures: 2015 spend on Sub-component #3 = $117M; 2012 spend = $14.25M. Reduction in cost = savings in profit. New 2015 total cost and new 2015 profit can be calculated.

math.setup: 2015 Sub-component #3 spend = $117M (39% x $300M). 2012 Sub-component #3 spend = $14.25M (25% x $57M). Reduction = $117M - $14.25M. New profit = old profit + reduction.
steps: vs. actual 2015 profit of $400M — an increase of $102.75M
math.answer: PrimeCo's 2015 profit would increase by $102.75M, rising from $400M to $502.75M.

brainstorming.prompt: The final recommendation should address not only the impact on profits but also broader strategic and financial considerations. What factors should PrimeCo take into account?

categories.name: Strategic implications
ideas: Once PrimeCo commits to improving SubPrime Co's operations, how will this affect relations with the producers of Sub-components #1 and #2?
Will other suppliers expect similar support or price negotiations?
What precedent does this set for PrimeCo's supplier relationships?
Could SubPrime Co become a strategic bottleneck if PrimeCo becomes too dependent?

categories.name: Financial implications for PrimeCo
ideas: What will PrimeCo have to invest to help SubPrime Co achieve reduced overhead and labor costs?
Will PrimeCo need to fund capital equipment, training, or process redesign at SubPrime Co?
What is the timeline to realize cost savings, and what is the payback period?

categories.name: Financial implications for SubPrime Co
ideas: What will SubPrime Co have to invest internally to achieve the reduced costs?
Can SubPrime Co sustain profitability at the new 15% margin with the lower price?
Is SubPrime Co financially healthy enough to make the required investments?

categories.name: Operational considerations
ideas: How quickly can SubPrime Co ramp down overhead costs?
What manufacturing best-practices can PrimeCo realistically share?
Are there risks of production disruption during the transition?

recommendation: PrimeCo's profit decline is driven by a dramatic increase in Sub-component #3 costs, which grew from $14.25M in 2012 to $117M in 2015, due to over-market pricing and inflated overhead at supplier SubPrime Co.

PrimeCo should proceed with the proposed deal: help SubPrime Co source Parts A, B, C at worldwide market prices and reduce overhead to industry average, resulting in a $1.00/unit price reduction to $9.00/unit.
If implemented, this could return Sub-component #3 spend to 2012 levels, increasing PrimeCo's 2015 profits by approximately $102.75M (from $400M to $502.75M).
risks: Investment cost to PrimeCo of supporting SubPrime Co's operational improvements is unknown and could offset savings
Other suppliers (Sub-components #1 and #2) may seek similar deals or feel disadvantaged
SubPrime Co may struggle to implement changes fast enough or at all
Dependence on a single nearby supplier creates concentration risk
next_steps: Conduct detailed due diligence on SubPrime Co's financials and operational improvement capacity
Estimate PrimeCo's investment required to support SubPrime Co's overhead and labor reduction
Model the timeline and phased cost savings to establish a payback period
Assess contractual and relationship implications with other sub-component suppliers
Explore whether partial in-sourcing of Sub-component #3 is a viable alternative
